content: The 60-day follow-up investigations for non-polio acute flaccid paralysis (NPAFP) cases in children aged 6–59 months were completed. The percentage of NPAFP cases was analyzed based on the number of polio vaccine doses received (0, 1–2, or ≥3). Epidemiological curves were created to classify cases by geographical area and year, while spot maps were used to identify confirmed cases by poliovirus type (WPV1/3, VDPV1/2/3), polio-compatible cases, and positive environmental surveillance (ES) samples. The proportion of subnational areas meeting two key surveillance indicators—NPAFP rate targets and stool adequacy rate—was assessed. These indicators are critical for evaluating the quality of disease surveillance and laboratory performance. In 2021, field and logistical activity indicators were reviewed, updated, and categorized into core and non-core indicators. The gold standard indicators for assessing acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance quality remain the non-polio AFP rate and stool adequacy. Timeliness of activities is crucial, including the detection of WPV/VDPV cases (final laboratory results within 35 days of onset), notification of cases (within 7 days of paralysis onset), investigation (within 48 hours of notification), and sample collection (two samples collected ≥24 hours apart within 14 days of paralysis onset). Delays in detection at any stage—field, laboratory, or logistical—can negatively impact outbreak response and increase transmission. Countries must monitor timeliness at every stage and address bottlenecks through regular analyses and reviews. Surveillance performance should be monitored using standard indicators, with a focus on areas of low performance. High-risk areas should be identified and prioritized for strengthening routine immunization and supplementary immunization activities (SIA). Surveillance coverage should be reviewed at national and subnational levels during quarterly EPI data review meetings to identify gaps and areas needing improvement. Comprehensive national surveillance reviews should be conducted every five years, with provincial reviews in larger countries ensuring all provinces are covered within the same timeframe. In the event of WPV, VDPV, or Sabin-like 2 virus isolation, immediate reporting to WHO is mandatory, regardless of the source (clinical case, environmental sample, etc.). Detection of WPV in an area must be followed by a timely response, including epidemiological investigation, enhanced AFP surveillance, and immediate immunization activities. Environmental surveillance (ES) plays a complementary role to AFP surveillance, particularly in areas with suboptimal AFP surveillance or high vaccination coverage. ES can detect poliovirus circulation, monitor the effectiveness of vaccination campaigns, and confirm the end of outbreaks. ES sampling sites should be selected based on population risk, sewage convergence, and minimal interference with virus detection. Sampling frequency should be at least once a month for routine sites, with temporary sites established during outbreaks for targeted populations. Samples must be collected, packaged, and transported under strict biosafety and cold chain conditions to preserve enteroviruses for laboratory testing. Samples should reach the laboratory within three days of collection, or seven days for international shipments. Supervision of ES activities is essential to maintain high-quality standards. On-site supervision should occur for at least 80% of sample collections quarterly, with documentation of these activities. Data collection and management tools are available to facilitate site registration, sample tracking, and result reporting. Environmental sites should undergo a validation period of 6–12 months before being formally included in the surveillance network. Decisions to close sites should involve thorough investigations and consultations with WHO regional offices, ensuring alignment with program needs and performance criteria. In summary, effective polio surveillance relies on a combination of AFP and ES systems, robust monitoring of performance indicators, timely detection and response to cases, and adherence to high-quality standards in sample collection, transport, and laboratory testing.
